title: ACGME Duty Hour Rules Every Residency Schedule Must Follow
description: The six ACGME work hour rules a residency schedule has to satisfy, in plain language, with the question to ask about each before you trust a schedule.
content:
Summary

  • Many scheduling tools fail to enforce specific ACGME rules like the 4-week rolling average for the 80-hour work week, which is where programs get caught out.
  • Most software is reactive, only flagging violations after a schedule is built, creating a frustrating cycle of manual fixes.
  • Use the six specific questions in this article to audit any vendor on their ability to proactively prevent violations, not just report them.
  • A managed service like Scheduling Wizard eliminates this problem by delivering a built in, ACGME-compliant schedule from the start.

If you've spent time in residency forums or talked candidly with chief residents, you already know the frustration. Programs are under enormous pressure to stay ACGME-compliant, yet residents frequently report feeling like the rules are more of a suggestion than a hard requirement, "[they] can make all the weak-ass recommendations they want, and programs ignore them without any serious repercussions," as one resident put it on Reddit.

The consequences of non-compliance aren't theoretical. They land on the residents first, in weeks nobody wanted and recovery time nobody planned for, and then on the program. When the stakes are this high, whoever builds the schedule, a chief, a vendor or a service, needs to show how each rule was handled, not just claim compliance.

This article isn't a rehash of the ACGME's duty hour rules. You already know the rules exist. What you need is a practical framework to ask any scheduling vendor, or anyone who builds schedules, how they actually handle them. For each of the six core duty hour requirements, we'll explain the rule in plain language and give you the specific question you should be asking every vendor you evaluate.

Let's get into it.

The 6 Core ACGME Duty Hour Rules Every Scheduling Tool Must Handle

The following six rules are based on the ACGME Common Program Requirements and form the basis of a compliant residency schedule.

1. The 80-Hour Weekly Limit (Averaged Over Four Weeks)

The Rule: Residents cannot work more than 80 hours per week. The critical nuance, which many tools quietly gloss over, is that this limit is calculated as an average over a four-week period, not as a hard cap on any single week. This means a resident could, technically, work more than 80 hours in one week as long as the four-week rolling average stays at or below 80 hours.

The Vendor Question to Ask:

"Does your tool calculate rolling 80-hour averages over a four-week period, or does it only check for violations in weekly snapshots?"

A tool that only checks week-by-week can miss violations the weekly view does not show. A resident who works 88 hours one week might look fine in isolation, but only a rolling four-week average calculation will tell you whether the program is actually compliant. If a vendor can't clearly explain how they handle this averaging, that's a red flag.

2. Rest Between Shifts: The Eight-Hour Guidance

The Rule: Residents should have at least eight hours off between scheduled duty periods, and the requirement is worded as a should rather than a must. After 24 hours of in-house call, residents must have at least 14 hours free. Those are two different rules, one a recommendation and one a hard requirement, and schedules get built wrong in both directions: treating the eight as optional, or forgetting that the 14 is not.

The Vendor Question to Ask:

"Does your tool keep eight hours off between scheduled work periods, and 14 hours after 24-hour call? Can it show me where a schedule meets the minimum but cuts it close, so I can make an informed trade-off?"

There is a difference between a tool that warns you after you have created the problem and one that does not let you create it. Either way, the eight hours should be visible in the build, so you know where a schedule sits: compliant, or compliant but cutting it close.

3. One Day Off in Seven (Averaged Over Four Weeks)

The Rule: Residents must have at least one continuous 24-hour period free from all clinical and educational duties every week. Like the 80-hour rule, this is averaged over a four-week period, so the requirement isn't strictly one day off per calendar week, but rather that the average over the block works out to at least one day in seven.

The Vendor Question to Ask:

"How does your tool track the 'one-in-seven' day-off requirement across its four-week averaging window? Can it detect and prevent scenarios where a resident is scheduled for more than six consecutive days of work?"

Applying a simple "one day off per week" rule is not the same as correctly implementing the four-week averaged version. These are different calculations, and a tool that conflates them can pass its own compliance checks while the program is actually in violation. Make sure you understand exactly how the math is being done.

4. In-House Call No More Than Every Third Night (Averaged Over Four Weeks)

The Rule: In-house call must be scheduled no more often than every third night, averaged over four weeks. At-home call is not subject to this limit, but any clinical work done while on at-home call counts toward the 80 hours, and at-home call cannot be assigned on a resident's free day.

The Vendor Question to Ask:

"How does your tool count call frequency when someone covers a sick colleague, and does it keep in-house call and at-home call separate?"

A q3 average that holds on paper breaks the first time a resident picks up a colleague's night. A tool that only checks the published schedule, not the schedule after swaps, will not see it.

5. The 24+4 Rule for All Residents

The rule: All residents, including PGY-1s, may be scheduled for up to 24 hours of continuous clinical work, with up to four additional hours for transitions of care and education. No new patient care can be assigned in those four hours. PGY-1s had a separate 16-hour cap until the 2017 revision removed it; since then the 24+4 standard applies at every PGY level.

The Vendor Question to Ask:

"Does your tool hold the 24-hour limit on scheduled work at every PGY level, and does it keep the +4 window free of new assignments?"

Any vendor still modelling a 16-hour PGY-1 cap is working from pre-2017 rules. The 2017 revision also made clear that clinical work from home, including at-home call activity, counts toward the 80 hours. The February 2026 interim revision did not change any of this; it suspended enforcement of a few requirements, including the 88-hour rotation exception, while a larger revision is prepared. If a vendor describes 2026 as the year home call started counting, they are a few years behind.

6. Moonlighting Hours Are Not Optional to Track

The Rule: All moonlighting hours, whether internal (within the sponsoring institution) or external (at outside facilities), must be counted toward the resident's 80-hour weekly average. The program is responsible for ensuring these hours are tracked and included in the total. Ignorance isn't a valid defense during an ACGME site visit.

The Vendor Question to Ask:

"What mechanism does your system provide for logging internal and external moonlighting hours? How are those hours automatically incorporated into the rolling 80-hour average calculation?"

If a tool can't easily ingest moonlighting data and fold it into the compliance calculation, then the program coordinator is stuck doing that math manually, which defeats a large part of the automation's value and introduces serious room for error. The system should treat a logged moonlighting hour exactly the same as a scheduled clinical hour for the purposes of the 80-hour limit.

The Compliance Gap: Proactive Prevention vs. Reactive Flagging

Here's the honest truth about most scheduling software on the market today: it's reactive. You build the schedule, run a compliance check, and the tool hands you back a list of violations, "Dr. Martinez has a rest period violation on Thursday," "Dr. Chen exceeds the 80-hour average in week 3." Then you're left manually untangling the schedule, usually under deadline pressure, trying to figure out which shifts to move without creating new problems in the process.

This is a fundamentally backwards workflow. You've already done the hard work of building a schedule, and now you have to partially rebuild it. Worse, there's always the risk that a corrected violation introduces a new one that the system catches on the next pass, and so on, in a frustrating loop.

The reactive model also puts enormous cognitive burden on whoever is doing the scheduling. For chief residents, who typically take on this responsibility without formal training, it's one of the most stressful parts of the role. For program coordinators, it means every schedule cycle ends with a scramble.

The alternative is a system that doesn't create violations in the first place.

How Managed Scheduling Handles This Differently

Rather than catching errors after schedule generation, a better approach puts all the ACGME duty hour rules into the schedule during the build, so the output was built to them rather than corrected afterwards.

This is how Scheduling Wizard works. We are a managed scheduling service; our team builds the schedule with every one of these requirements in it from the start: the rolling 80-hour average, eight hours off between scheduled periods, 14 hours after 24-hour call, one day in seven, the 24+4 limit at every PGY level, in-house call no more than every third night, and clinical work from home and moonlighting counted toward the 80. Because the rules go in while the schedule is built, there is far less to find afterwards. We are people, not a guarantee, and we say so; what we can say is that the rules were built in rather than checked for.

But the bigger differentiator isn't the schedule itself, it's the model. Scheduling Wizard is a done-for-you managed service, not self-service software. Programs submit their rules (coverage requirements, rotation assignments, vacation requests, individual preferences, moonlighting plans), and Scheduling Wizard's team delivers the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for whatever platform the program already uses day to day. No software to learn. No interface to navigate.

This managed service model also solves a problem that doesn't get talked about enough: institutional scheduling continuity. When the chief resident who built last year's schedule rotates out, their knowledge of all the edge cases, the informal program rules, and the hard-won workarounds leaves with them. With a service like Scheduling Wizard, that logic stays with us and persists year after year, regardless of who holds the chief title.

Demand a Schedule, Not Just a Validator

When you're evaluating ACGME compliant scheduling software, the right standard isn't "does it catch my errors?" The right standard is "does it make errors impossible?" Tools that flag violations are better than nothing, but they still leave compliance as a reactive, manual process. The strongest option is a system, or service, that builds the rules in while the schedule is built before the schedule is ever published.

Use the six vendor questions above as your audit framework. Push every vendor on the specifics. If they can't clearly explain how they handle rolling averages, call frequency after swaps, and the 24+4 rule at every PGY level, you have your answer.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Scheduling Wizard and platforms like Amion?

Scheduling Wizard is a managed scheduling service that builds your ACGME-compliant schedule for you, whereas platforms like Amion and QGenda are self-service software primarily used for viewing and day-to-day communication of an already-built schedule. We deliver the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you; most programs upload it to the platform they already use. We work alongside these tools, not as a direct replacement.

How does Scheduling Wizard ensure compliance with my specialty's specific ACGME rules?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we build them into the schedule alongside your own rules. We do not assume we know your specialty's requirements better than you do; we ask, write them down with you, and build to them.

Did the February 2026 ACGME revision change the work hour rules?

Less than the headlines suggested. The February 2026 interim revision of the Common Program Requirements did not change the work hour limits; it suspended enforcement of a handful of requirements, including the rotation-specific 88-hour exception, while the ACGME prepares a major revision (a draft was posted for comment in September 2026 with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2028; nothing in it applies yet). The rules a schedule is built to today are the ones in place since the 2017 revision: 80 hours a week averaged over four weeks, with clinical work from home, at-home call activity and moonlighting all counted; no more than 24 hours of continuous scheduled work plus up to four for transitions, at every PGY level; at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call; one day in seven free, averaged over four weeks, with no at-home call on those days; and in-house call no more often than every third night. We build to the rules in force, and when they change we rebuild to the new ones.

Why is building the rules in better than flagging violations afterward?

Building the rules in is better because it prevents ACGME violations from ever being created, saving significant time and reducing compliance risk. Reactive tools only flag violations after you've built the schedule, forcing you into a frustrating cycle of manual fixes. We build the schedule with the rules in it from the start, so the back-and-forth is about preferences and trade-offs, not about fixing violations.

What happens if we need to make last-minute changes to the schedule?

Last-minute changes are a reality in residency programs, and we have a process to accommodate them. Day-to-day swaps stay with the program. When something bigger happens, a leave, a rotation change, a coverage gap, you tell us and we rebuild the schedule around it with the same rules in place. Redrafts through the year are part of the service.

What do I receive from Scheduling Wizard, and how do I use it?

You receive the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Most programs upload it into whatever platform their residents already use for daily viewing. The process is simple: you provide us with your requirements (rotations, vacations, rules), and we return a finished schedule. There is no software for you to learn or manage.
